title: Europe's Overseas Countries and Territories as Geopolitical Assets
gist: A Carnegie Europe survey of Europe's 30 Overseas Countries and Territories (OCTs) identifies seven as strategically contested 'bastions' (Diego Garcia/Chagos, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, Gibraltar, Greenland, New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna) where US, Chinese, and Russian predatory pressure — via military threats, financial investment, or outright territorial claims — is testing Europe's fragmented, rules-based diplomatic architecture, which the author argues cannot match rivals' fait-accompli tactics but must resist them anyway.

themes.theme: Greenland as the paradigm case of great-power pressure on a European OCT

insights.claim: Greenland's ice sheet holds 25 of the 34 minerals the European Commission classifies as 'critical,' including rare-earth elements, graphite, and lithium, yet extraction is hampered by the climate, ice-sheet depth, absence of roads, and Greenland's legal mining framework; Australian, Chinese, and US mining companies already hold extraction permits from Greenlandic authorities.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Greenland is a live, multi-permit-holder critical-minerals frontier despite operational difficulty — relevant to critical-minerals supply-chain diversification plays and to monitoring which miners (Australian/Chinese/US) gain first-mover extraction advantage as ice-sheet access improves.
insights.locator: Section on Greenland, mineral reserves paragraph

insights.claim: President Trump has repeatedly claimed since March 2025 that the US should 'own' or 'get' Greenland for security reasons, renewing the claim at the July 2026 NATO Ankara summit even as Danish PM Mette Frederiksen reiterated her opposition; this triggered a still-unresolved EU legal debate over whether NATO's mutual-assistance clause applies to Greenland as a Danish OCT.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: An unresolved legal ambiguity over NATO's mutual-defense obligations toward an OCT is a novel, underpriced geopolitical tail risk for European security markets and Danish sovereign risk premia.
insights.quote: Countries have to have ownership and you defend ownership, you don’t defend leases. And we’ll have to defend Greenland.
insights.locator: Section on Greenland, Trump quote on ownership

insights.claim: Greenland receives 45% of the EU's entire 2021-2027 financial program for Overseas Countries and Territories, with priorities spanning education, renewable energy, digital connectivity, critical raw materials, sustainable tourism, and environmental research.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Quantifies the EU's outsized financial commitment to Greenland relative to its 29 OCT peers, underscoring how central Greenland has become to EU strategic and industrial policy even before accounting for the US pressure campaign.
insights.locator: Section on Greenland, EU financial program paragraph

themes.theme: Diego Garcia/Chagos: a base contested between allies

insights.claim: The UK began returning the Chagos Islands (British Indian Ocean Territory) to Mauritius in 2022, reaching a May 2025 agreement that kept the Diego Garcia air/naval base under British-US control; the US initially strongly praised the deal but in 2026 challenged the process, complicated by Iran's attempted intercontinental missile strike on the archipelago in late March 2026 — the UK parliament's ratification has been suspended since April 2026.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: A key US-UK military base's sovereignty status remains legally unresolved amid an active Iranian missile threat, creating a live UK-US alliance friction point and a base-continuity risk for Middle East/Indo-Pacific power projection.
insights.locator: Section on British Indian Ocean Territory / Diego Garcia

insights.claim: President Trump has separately threatened to 'buy back' Diego Garcia, using the same rhetorical playbook (public social-media-style ownership claims) he applied to Greenland.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Establishes a recurring Trump-administration pattern of asserting ownership claims over allied strategic territories — useful for anticipating similar rhetoric toward other overseas bases (e.g., Panama Canal-style precedent) and its market-moving potential.
insights.locator: Section on Trump's Diego Garcia comments

themes.theme: New Caledonia's nickel and the China-Pacific contest

insights.claim: New Caledonia possesses the world's third-largest proven nickel ore deposit after Indonesia and the Philippines, and despite high production costs, maintaining its mining/processing operations is a strategic objective of the French government, which continues monitoring China's expanding economic and military presence in the Pacific.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: France is willing to subsidize an uneconomic nickel operation for strategic reasons — relevant for battery/EV supply-chain analysts tracking non-market-driven nickel supply and for gauging France's tolerance for state support of critical-minerals production.

themes.theme: China's fait-accompli playbook beyond the OCTs

insights.claim: The author frames China's investments in the Port of Piraeus (Greece) and France's Toulouse airport (which hosts a major Airbus plant) as examples of a broader Chinese pattern of financial-investment-based influence-building in strategic European locations, even though these specific cases have not touched European OCTs directly.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Signals that Chinese strategic-asset acquisition in Europe operates through ostensibly commercial channels near sensitive industrial sites (e.g., Airbus production) — a template investors should watch for replication in or near other OCT-adjacent supply chains.
insights.locator: Section: The Geopolitical Importance of Europe's OCTs, China paragraph

insights.claim: China maintained a military presence in the Arabian Sea during the 2026 US-Israeli war on Iran, in addition to its established pattern of building artificial islands in the South China Sea — part of what the author calls a range of overseas techniques short of territorial annexation.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Documents China projecting naval presence into an active Middle East conflict zone (2026 Iran war) — relevant context for assessing Chinese power-projection ambitions beyond its immediate region.
insights.locator: Section: The Geopolitical Importance of Europe's OCTs, China military presence

themes.theme: Europe's structural disadvantage in fait-accompli geopolitics

insights.claim: The author's core framework: China, Russia, and the US each pursue their own distinct 'diplomatic fait accompli' by combining public/private financial power, military force, propaganda, and defiance of established international rules — a toolkit that Western Europe, constrained by rule-of-law, national constitutions, and EU/Council of Europe treaty procedures, cannot and does not replicate, leaving it structurally reactive and often caught off guard.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: A durable asymmetry thesis: expect Europe to continue responding to territorial/strategic pressure through slow legal and diplomatic channels rather than matching rivals' speed — a structural handicap relevant to any scenario analysis of contested European assets (Greenland, Gibraltar, Chagos).
insights.quote: By combining public and private financial means, economic strategy, military force, propaganda, and the defiance of long-established rules of international behavior, these states have been able to push their preferred policies through the community of nations—friends and foes alike.
insights.locator: Section: A Diplomatic Fait Accompli vs. Europe's Democratic Architecture

insights.claim: The November 2025 US National Security Strategy formally expressed a policy openly hostile to America's previous European allies, souring transatlantic relations since January 20, 2025; European governments have since found some ways to react collectively but remain vulnerable to personal attacks and are not always united.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Documents a formalized, doctrine-level shift in US posture toward Europe (not just rhetoric), a structural input for reassessing transatlantic security-alliance risk premia and EU strategic-autonomy investment themes (defense industrials, EU-only supply chains).
insights.locator: Section: A Diplomatic Fait Accompli, paragraph on 2025 National Security Strategy

insights.claim: The author argues there is no single legal or diplomatic template for defending OCTs from external interference — cases range from purely national/hypothetical (New Caledonia) to involving only a handful of interlocutors (British Indian Ocean Territory) to implicating an entire EU member state's obligations (Greenland) — but all such disruptive actions ultimately fracture European democratic architecture and should be systematically resisted.
insights.speaker: Marc Pierini
insights.so_what: Warns against a one-size-fits-all EU policy response to OCT threats — investors and policymakers should expect case-by-case, potentially slow and inconsistent EU reactions depending on which member state and legal framework is implicated.
insights.quote: No cajoling of or pandering to disruptive foreign forces will ever protect European democracy.
